cases.rationale: Bf8+ makes the bishop trade on b4 available. Be3 and Kb1 preserve different bishop activity and plans against the connected queenside pawns.
Both sides contest the f-file and can exchange on f3. Be3 and Bf2 alter which side maintains pressure.
Rc1 and Rae1 change the possible rook and queen captures. After Bxf6 gxf6 the g-file and doubled f-pawns change king safety.
The second-rank rook can be traded or contained by the king. The g-pawn exchanges change the initiative on the g-file.
...exf5 allows Nxf5+ and Nxh6. ...f6, ...Nbc6 and ...b6 also change the central pawn tension and blockade.
White has to answer the second-rank rook. The central pawn chain and the d6 knight persist after the possible rook exchanges.
After ...exd5, Rf2 threatens Rfxb2. ...Nd6 keeps coordination behind the b2 passer, which governs the placements.
Three ways to take on d4 or d5 lead to distinct sequences involving e4, d3 or the e-file. The independent value of the resulting pawn structure is unclear.
Qxb3 Nc5+ and Rd2 lead to the forcing queen-for-rook sequence. Ke2 lets the knights attack b2 and the queen check on d3.
...b5, ...f6 and ...g6 expand in different ways from the e4 pawn and the knight on d3. Queenside pressure remains when trades are delayed.
Nc5 allows ...axb4 and ...Nxd4. In the sounder queen lines, the long-term c4 outpost and queenside pawn breaks govern the continuation.
Trading on a2, centralizing through d6 or keeping the rooks active are viable. The a-file and the c5 knight govern the play.
The stronger moves preserve checking resources. Qe2 allows a queen exchange into a pawn-down ending without these checks.
...exf3 starts a concrete sequence on f3 including two rook exchanges and ...Rxc4. The alternatives let the knight escape.
...Rfc8 permits Rxc8+ and Bxa6. The bishop routes avoid that sequence and the f- and b-pawn levers stay important.
The knight captures on e5 allow different exchanges including ...Nxd4. The pawn capture changes the centre and leaves rooks competing for the c-file.
...f6 changes the defence of e4 and permits a queen-and-rook sequence. ...Nf6 preserves different central coordination after the queens come off.
Re3 and Ba3 transpose into an exchange and defence of e4. White's g-pawn advance and central squares still govern piece coordination.
...h4 prevents h4+ and changes the king's escape. The bishop also reorganizes the pieces around d5 and e5 in the viable lines.
...Nxe8 takes the exposed rook. ...Rxh4+ is answered by a king move and Nxg4+. The exchanges and checks govern the decision.
...Rb1 allows Qb5+ and the f-pawn captures. The better moves keep both rooks active against the advancing b-pawn.
...f5 and the knight route to d5 after ...Ra7 are long-term choices. ...Qb7 and ...Rc8 can trade queens while retaining c-file play.
...f5 allows exf5 and ...Bxd5, before Ng5 threatens near the king. After the queen trade the lasting contribution is uncertain.
...Nxa4 can initiate the c-file liquidation. The alternatives also change which side can contest the seventh rank afterward.
The defence must account for g5 and Qh5 around the king. ...Nf8 and the g-pawn advance also change control over f4 and h4 long term.
The queen moves change whether h5 is lost via a queen exchange. The h4 knight and f-pawn break stay important afterward.
Bd6 allows ...Rxd6 and liquidation. The f- and e-pawn captures, or h6, change king cover and White's advanced pawn structure.
Qf4 permits a queen exchange and rook activity. The quiet alternatives attack the same central structure with queen and rook maneuvering.

limitations: One engine-assisted reviewer used legal leading continuations and ordinary reply probes without classifier output or optional position replies.
Cases are paired broadcast losses and controls from 14 games across two tournaments and do not estimate prevalence.
Uncertain axes are null. The legacy proxy uses its motif on the first engine choice and has no independent positional axis.
